Roughear scad (Decapterus tabl) attains a maximum recorded body length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a measurement derived from extensive fishery surveys across its tropical distribution range. This ultimate total length represents the largest individuals encountered in commercial catches, though adults more typically range between 40 and 45 centimeters. The species exhibits a robust, fusiform body plan well-suited to sustained pelagic cruising, with a laterally compressed caudal peduncle reinforced by lateral keels. Sexual maturation in this carangid begins when individuals reach approximately 30 centimeters [Lp = approximately 30 centimeters] in total length, a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal development and the capacity for reproductive contribution. Field studies indicate that length at puberty is a more reliable indicator of maturation than age in this species, given the considerable variation in growth rates across its latitudinal range. Juvenile specimens recruit to pelagic schools before attaining this size and undergo a period of rapid somatic growth prior to the allocation of resources toward gamete production.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C], hatching of Roughear scad embryos occurs approximately seven days [ab = approximately seven days] after fertilisation. This brief embryonic duration is characteristic of tropical carangids and reflects the elevated metabolic rates sustained at warm water temperatures. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a dry weight at birth of only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly one millimeter that typifies the genus Decapterus. These lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, undergoing rapid differentiation of the digestive tract and visual system before the onset of exogenous feeding. The low initial mass imposes a narrow window for successful first feeding, as larvae must locate suitable planktonic prey before yolk absorption is complete. Mortality rates during this transitional period are consequently high, representing a critical bottleneck in early life history.

At a water temperature of 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C], gravid females release between 400 and 420 oocytes per day [Ri = between 400 and 420 oocytes per day], representing the maximum daily reproductive output recorded for the species. This high fecundity is sustained over an extended spawning season, with females participating in repeated spawning events across several months. The combination of moderate clutch size and protracted spawning frequency results in a substantial lifetime reproductive investment, with individual females capable of producing tens of thousands of oocytes over a single reproductive season. Environmental cues such as photoperiod and temperature appear to modulate the timing and intensity of spawning activity, with peak reproductive effort coinciding with periods of elevated primary productivity.

Adults of Roughear scad reach a maximum wet body mass of 1599 grams [Wwi = 1599 grams], a figure derived from length-weight relationships established through extensive sampling of commercial landings. This ultimate wet weight is attained relatively early in the lifespan, as growth decelerates markedly following the onset of reproductive maturity. The length-weight relationship follows a standard allometric form typical of fusiform pelagic fishes, with exponent values close to 3. At the onset of reproductive maturity, individuals weighing approximately 343.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 343.6 grams] redirect a portion of assimilated energy toward gonadal development and spawning activity. This mass threshold at puberty represents roughly one-fifth of the maximum attainable body mass, a ratio consistent with patterns observed in other iteroparous carangids that exhibit moderate fecundity and extended reproductive lifespans. Body condition indices fluctuate seasonally in relation to spawning cycles and prey availability.

Longevity in Decapterus tabl has been estimated through otolith-based ageing studies, which indicate a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] at 16.6 °C [T = 16.6 °C]. This translates to approximately five years, a moderate lifespan for a pelagic carangid of its body size. Mortality schedules are shaped by both natural predation pressure and fishing exploitation, with the species forming an important component of artisanal and commercial fisheries throughout its range. The sustained growth trajectory during the first two years of life allows individuals to reach a size refuge from many piscine predators, though they remain vulnerable to larger tunas and billfishes. Comparisons with congeneric species suggest that lifespan may be shorter at the warmer edge of the species distribution and slightly extended in cooler, higher-latitude populations, reflecting the metabolic theory of ecology's predictions for temperature-dependent aging rates.
